claim: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common form of lung cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related death in Australia.
source: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common form of lung cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related death in Australia.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact presented in the introduction without specific citation, drawing on established medical knowledge.

claim: Less than 15% of LUAD patients have a targetable driver mutation.
source: Less than 15% of patients have a targetable driver mutation and therefore cannot benefit from targeted therapy (Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herbst et al., 2018.

claim: The overwhelming majority of LUAD patients receive platinum-based chemotherapy as standard of care.
source: Consequently, the overwhelming majority of LUAD patients receive platinum-based chemotherapy as standard of care.
evidence: This follows logically from the previous statement about lack of targetable mutations and represents established clinical practice.

claim: The anti-tumour abilities of platinum compounds were first identified over 50 years ago with the discovery of cisplatin.
source: The anti-tumour abilities of platinum compounds were first identified over 50 years ago with the discovery of cisplatin (Kelland, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelland, 2007.

claim: Platinum therapy is essentially curative in testicular cancer, with survival rates > 90%.
source: Platinum therapy is essentially curative in testicular cancer, with survival rates > 90%, and is also a frontline treatment for small-cell lung cancer, ovarian, head and neck, bladder, and cervical cancers (Gonzalez-Rajal et al., 2020; Kelland, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gonzalez-Rajal et al., 2020 and Kelland, 2007.

claim: Response rates to platinum in LUAD are below 30%, due primarily to innate resistance.
source: Unfortunately, response rates to platinum in LUAD are below 30%, due primarily to innate resistance (Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herbst et al., 2018.

claim: Nearly 150 different mechanisms of platinum resistance have been identified to date.
source: Nearly 150 different mechanisms of platinum resistance have been identified to date (Stewart, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stewart, 2007.

claim: Cisplatin reaches a peak plasma concentration of ~14 µM (5 µg/ml) in patients, which is then rapidly cleared by the kidneys within 2–4 hr.
source: Cisplatin is given to patients as a single bolus dose, reaching a peak plasma concentration of ~14 µM (5 µg/ml), which is then rapidly cleared by the kidneys within 2–4 hr (Andersson et al., 1996; Urien and Lokiec, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andersson et al., 1996 and Urien and Lokiec, 2004.

claim: The authors mimicked in vivo cisplatin exposure in vitro by pulsing cells for 2 hr with the maximum plasma concentration.
source: We therefore mimicked this in vitro by pulsing cells for 2 hr with the maximum plasma concentration (Hastings et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in this study and references prior work (Hastings et al., 2020).

claim: The binding of platinum compounds to DNA, which forms platinum-DNA adducts, is thought to be the primary mechanism for their tumour-specific killing.
source: Once inside cells, platinum compounds can bind to DNA, RNA, and proteins (Gonzalez-Rajal et al., 2020); however, the binding to DNA, which forms platinum-DNA adducts, is thought to be the primary mechanism for their tumour-specific killing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez-Rajal et al., 2020 and represents established understanding in the field.

claim: Intra-strand DNA-platinum adducts are repaired by base excision and nucleotide excision repair during G1.
source: Intra-strand DNA-platinum adducts are repaired by base excision and nucleotide excision repair during G1 (Slyskova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Slyskova et al., 2018.

claim: Inter-strand crosslinks (ICLs) are removed largely by the Fanconi anaemia (FA) pathway.
source: Inter-strand crosslinks (ICLs) are removed largely by the Fanconi anaemia (FA) pathway (Smogorzewska, 2019), which generates single- and double-strand breaks that are resolved by either the high-fidelity homologous recombination (HR) pathway during S phase (Karanam et al., 2012) or by the error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway during G1 and G2 phase (Enoiu et al., 2012; Slyskova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smogorzewska, 2019; Karanam et al., 2012; Enoiu et al., 2012; and Slyskova et al., 2018.

claim: Cells with defective HR repair have been shown to be highly sensitive to combination therapy with cisplatin and PARP inhibitors in ovarian and breast cancer.
source: For example, cells with defective HR repair have been shown to be highly sensitive to combination therapy with cisplatin and PARP inhibitors in a number of cancer types, including ovarian and breast (Tutt et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tutt et al., 2018.

claim: Correlation between cisplatin sensitivity and impaired DNA repair has often failed to translate clinically in LUAD.
source: However, correlation between cisplatin sensitivity and impaired DNA repair has often failed to translate clinically in LUAD (Mamdani and Jalal, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mamdani and Jalal, 2016.

claim: TGF-β and P70S6K have been identified as key mediators of innate platinum resistance in LUAD.
source: In contrast, we have recently identified TGF-β (Marini et al., 2018) and P70S6K (Hastings et al., 2020) as key mediators of innate platinum resistance in LUAD.
evidence: Supported by citations to Marini et al., 2018 and Hastings et al., 2020, representing the authors' prior work.

claim: A sub-population of cells in late G1/early S phase at the time of cisplatin exposure are capable of continued proliferation and can sufficiently repair their DNA over multiple generations.
source: Using a combination of cell cycle, DNA damage, and replication biosensors together with real-time single-cell fate tracking, we identified that these proliferative cells were enriched in late G1/early S phase at the time of cisplatin exposure and were able to sufficiently repair their DNA over multiple generations and rounds of replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The initial pulse of cisplatin blocked the proliferation of A549 and NCI-H1573 cells, and significantly reduced NCI-H1299 cell numbers over a 3-day period.
source: The initial pulse of cisplatin blocked the proliferation of A549 and NCI-H1573 cells, and significantly reduced NCI-H1299 cell numbers over a 3-day period.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cisplatin treatment resulted in a two- to sixfold increase in total cell and nuclear area across all three cell lines (A549, NCI-H1573, NCI-H1299).
source: Subsequent visual and quantitative analysis of cells by immunofluorescence revealed a corresponding two- to sixfold increase in total cell and nuclear area across all three cell lines (Figure 1C, D), accounting for the reduced impact on confluence.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Cells recovered to their pre-pulse size and normal cell cycle distribution over 7–21 days of recovery (42 days for NCI-H1573).
source: Over the following 7–21 days of recovery (42 days for NCI-H1573 due to slower rate of proliferation), cells eventually recovered to their pre-pulse size and normal cell cycle distribution (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C, D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Subsequent cisplatin pulse of recovered cultures resulted in a near identical response to the initial pulse.
source: In all three cell lines, subsequent cisplatin pulse of recovered cultures resulted in a near identical response to the initial pulse, both in terms of inhibition of cell number, reduced confluence, and increased cell size (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Cells surviving the first cisplatin exposure remained equally sensitive to cisplatin and were unlikely to have acquired resistance or arisen from an intrinsically resistant sub-clonal population.
source: Based on these results, and our previous observation that all cells contained significantly increased levels of cisplatin-DNA adducts (Hastings et al., 2020), we concluded that cells surviving the first exposure remained equally sensitive to cisplatin and were therefore unlikely to have acquired resistance or arisen from an intrinsically resistant sub-clonal population within each cell line.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and previous observations cited from Hastings et al., 2020.

claim: A significant increase in senescence associated beta-galactosidase (β-gal) staining was observed in A549 and to a lesser extent H1573 and H1299 cell lines after cisplatin treatment.
source: In support, a significant increase in senescence associated beta-galactosidase (β-gal) staining was observed both visually and by flow cytometry (C12FDG) in A549 and to a lesser extent H1573 and H1299 cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Increased levels of p16 were associated with larger cells in NCI-H1573 and H1299 cells, while in A549 cells, p21 was similarly increased.
source: Increased levels of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p16, which is commonly linked with senescence, was associated with larger cells in NCI-H1573 and H1299 cells, while in A549 cells, which are null for p16 (Kawabe et al., 2000), p21 was similarly increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citation to Kawabe et al., 2000.

claim: Larger cells after cisplatin treatment have a lower proliferative capacity and are likely senescent.
source: These data suggest that in each cell line the larger cells have a lower proliferative capacity and are likely senescent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the β-gal and p16/p21 data.

claim: Repopulation of the culture after the initial pulse exposure is primarily driven by a small fraction of cells.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that repopulation of the culture after the initial pulse exposure is primarily driven by a small fraction of cells, with the total number of clones impacted by p53 status.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LeGO RGB clonal tracking experiments shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: The total number of clones capable of repopulation after cisplatin exposure is impacted by p53 status.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that repopulation of the culture after the initial pulse exposure is primarily driven by a small fraction of cells, with the total number of clones impacted by p53 status.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that NCI-H1299 (p53 null) cells displayed greater variability in recovered clonal colours compared to A549 (p53 wt) and NCI-H1573 (p53 mutant) cells.

claim: All three cell lines showed a significant increase in cell size at 3 days post carboplatin treatment in vivo.
source: Mice harvested at 3 days post treatment were analysed by imunohistochemistry (IHC) for cell size and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA)-positive staining, with all cell lines showing a significant increase in cell size (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Active proliferation (PCNA positivity) in A549 cells was strongly suppressed after carboplatin exposure in vivo.
source: Similar to the in vitro results, active proliferation (PCNA positivity) in A549 cells was strongly suppressed after carboplatin exposure, indicating that the majority of cells were not proliferating.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: NCI-H1299 cells did not show any significant decrease in PCNA staining in vivo after carboplatin treatment.
source: In contrast, NCI-H1299 cells, which lack p53, did not show any significant decrease in PCNA staining in vivo (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Presence of functional p53 correlates with increased senescence and reduced active replication in enlarged cells after cisplatin exposure.
source: In summary, these in vitro and in vivo data suggest that in LUAD cells exposure to pulsed cisplatin results in a significant proportion of cells increasing in size, with presence of functional p53 correlating with increased senescence and reduced active replication in enlarged cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: A sub-population of cells remain at a normal (stable) cell size, maintain their proliferative capacity, and drive repopulation of the cell culture after cisplatin exposure.
source: Interestingly, in all three lines, a sub-population of cells remain at a normal (stable) cell size, maintained their proliferative capacity, and drove repopulation of the cell culture.
evidence: This is supported by the clonal tracking and cell size analysis data.

claim: Proliferative cells after cisplatin exposure remained equally sensitive to subsequent cisplatin treatment, indicating a non-genetic mechanism of resistance.
source: Despite this, these proliferative cells remained equally sensitive to subsequent cisplatin treatment, indicating a non-genetic mechanism of resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the re-challenge experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cisplatin-treated stable cells displayed a decrease in EIF2, mTOR, and p70S6K signalling, with a corresponding increase in TREM1, GP6, and IL-17F signalling pathways.
source: Notably, these stable cells displayed a decrease in EIF2, mTOR, and p70S6K signalling, with a corresponding increase in TREM1, GP6, and IL-17F signalling pathways (Figure 4F, Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4F and Supplementary files 3 and 4.

claim: Stable cisplatin-treated cells showed strong upregulation of BRCA1, ATM, and DNA replication signalling pathways, which were heavily suppressed in non-proliferative cells.
source: Four-way comparative analysis further highlighted key differences between each sub-population, with stable cells all showing strong upregulation of BRCA1, ATM, and DNA replication signalling pathways, which were heavily suppressed in non-proliferative cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) identified strong enrichment for cell cycle, HR-directed repair, ATR, and the Fanconi pathway in stable compared to enlarged cells.
source: Similarly, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) identified strong enrichment for cell cycle, HR-directed repair, ATR, and the Fanconi pathway in stable compared to enlarged cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Cisplatin-treated stable cells do not undergo significant p53/p21-dependent cell cycle checkpoint arrest but do show prominent upregulation of DNA repair pathways involving HR/BRCA1 and ATM/ATR.
source: In summary, these data suggest that the cisplatin-treated stable cells are considerably different from enlarged and untreated control cells. Specifically, stable cells do not undergo significant p53/p21-dependent cell cycle checkpoint arrest but do show prominent upregulation of DNA repair pathways involving HR/BRCA1 and ATM/ATR.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the RNAseq analysis.

claim: Cisplatin treatment resulted in a range of cell cycle perturbations including a significant and prolonged S/G2 phase arrest.
source: In contrast and as demonstrated previously (Hastings et al., 2020), cisplatin-treated cells showed a range of cell cycle perturbations (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), including a significant and prolonged S/G2 phase arrest (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which correlated with a reduced number of total divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C, and citation to Hastings et al., 2020.

claim: Cisplatin-treated cells that underwent multiple divisions within 72 hr were enriched for cells that were in late G1 and early S phase at the time of cisplatin exposure.
source: Combining this with additional scoring of cisplatin-treated cells that underwent multiple (two or more) divisions within the 72 hr period revealed an enrichment for cells that were in late G1 and early S phase at the time of cisplatin exposure (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Unbiased analysis of 400 cisplatin-treated A549 cells found a significant increase in the number of divisions arising from cells that were in G1/S or early S phase at the time of exposure compared to G1 phase cells.
source: Unbiased analysis of an additional 400 cisplatin-treated A549 cells found a significant increase in the number of divisions arising from cells that were in G1/S or early S phase at the time of exposure compared to G1 phase cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The overwhelming majority of cells in late S or G2/M only completed one division during the 72 hr period after cisplatin treatment.
source: Furthermore, the overwhelming majority of cells in late S or G2/M only completed one division during the 72 hr period.
evidence: This is supported by the single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is a cell cycle-dependent mechanism driving the ability of A549 cells to continue to proliferate after cisplatin exposure.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that there is a cell cycle-dependent mechanism driving the ability of A549 cells to continue to proliferate after cisplatin exposure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell cycle-dependent differences in proliferation observed in the FUCCI experiments.

claim: In vivo, approximately 70–80% of cells from each line were in G1 phase prior to cisplatin treatment.
source: Notably, prior to cisplatin treatment, approximately 70–80% of cells from each line were in G1 phase (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: In vivo, an increase in proportion of S/G2 phase cells was observed at day 1 after carboplatin treatment in all cell lines.
source: Similar to in vitro results, we observed an increase in proportion of S/G2 phase cells at day 1 in all cell lines, indicating that cells were arrested in S/G2.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: In A549 cells in vivo, over 90% of cells were in a G1 like state (red) at 7 days post carboplatin treatment.
source: In A549 cells, the percentage of S/G2 cells reduced gradually from day 3 to 7, resulting in over 90% of A549 cells in a G1 like state (red) at 7 days post treatment (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The presence of wild-type p53 (in A549 cells) corresponded with a higher rate of G2-exit and senescence compared to p53 null and mutant cells.
source: This mirrored our above in vitro data, where the presence of wild-type p53 (in A549 cells) corresponded with a higher rate of G2-exit and senescence compared to p53 null and mutant cells (Hastings et al., 2020), suggesting that the results we observed in vitro are recapitulated in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing in vivo and in vitro data, with citation to Hastings et al., 2020.

claim: Cells in late G1 and early S phase at the time of cisplatin exposure had a greater capacity to undergo multiple divisions compared to cells in G1 and S-G2/M phase.
source: The above data indicated that in p53 wild-type cells those in late G1 and early S phase at the time of exposure had a greater capacity to undergo multiple division compared to cells G1 and S-G2/M phase.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the FUCCI experiments.

claim: Targeting cells in G1 with cisplatin resulted in the majority of cells undergoing a prolonged S/G2 phase and then exiting back into a G1-like state without undergoing mitosis (G2-exit).
source: To target G1, cells were pulsed with cisplatin upon release from palbociclib (Cis at G1). This resulted in the majority of cells undergoing a prolonged S/G2 phase and then exiting back into a G1-like state without undergoing mitosis (G2-exit; Figure 6C), a state we described previously (Hastings et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6C and citation to Hastings et al., 2020.

claim: Only 7/50 cells targeted in G1 with cisplatin completed a single division, and no cells underwent multiple divisions during the 72 hr time period.
source: Notably, only 7/50 cells completed a single division, and no cells underwent multiple (two or more) divisions during the 72 hr time period (Figure 6A–D; proliferative).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Targeting cells in G1/S with cisplatin resulted in significantly more cells (13/50 and 16/50) completing two or more divisions.
source: In contrast, targeting cells in G1/S (Cis at G1/S) using either palbociclib or thymidine synchronisation with cisplatin resulted in significantly more cells (13/50 and 16/50, respectively) completing two or more divisions (Figure 6A–D; proliferative).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Nearly all cells targeted in late S phase with cisplatin completed the first mitosis and then underwent prolonged S/G2 arrest and G2-exit, with only 4 out of 50 cells completing two divisions within the 72 hr period.
source: Finally, nearly all cells targeted in late S phase (Cis at S) completed the first mitosis and then underwent prolonged S/G2 arrest and G2-exit, with only 4 out of 50 cells completing two divisions within the 72 hr period (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Cells in late G1 and early S phase at the time of cisplatin exposure have a greater capacity to continue proliferating.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that cells in late G1 and early S at the time of cisplatin exposure have a greater capacity to continue proliferating.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synchronization experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cells in late G1/early S phase were able to repair cisplatin-induced DNA damage during the first cell cycle more efficiently than cells in early G1 or late S phase.
source: We therefore hypothesised that cells in late G1/early S phase were able to repair cisplatin-induced DNA damage during the first cell cycle more efficiently than cells in early G1 or late S phase, thereby allowing them to continue proliferation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: In control cells, a small number (<20) of 53BP1-positive foci were observed as cells underwent the first round of replication.
source: In control cells, a small number (<20) of 53BP1-positive foci (red hot) were observed as cells underwent the first round of replication (Figure 7A, B, Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Cells that were in G1 at the time of cisplatin exposure entered S phase and rapidly accumulated a large number (~100) of 53BP1-positive foci.
source: Cells that were in G1 at the time of cisplatin exposure entered S phase and rapidly accumulated a large number (~100) of 53BP1-positive foci; these slowly reduced over the remainder of the time lapse (Figure 7A–C), which corresponded with an increase in the average size of the foci (~1 µm2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Cells that were in early S phase and completed multiple divisions showed a rapid rise in 53BP1 foci number (~100), which then decreased at the conclusion of S phase.
source: In contrast, cells that were in early S phase and completed multiple (two or more) divisions within the 72 hr timeframe showed a rapid rise in foci number (~100), which then decreased at the conclusion of S phase, correlating with an increase in foci size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: In grand-daughter and great grand-daughter cells from early S phase-treated cells, the size of G1 53BP1 foci increased (>2 µm2), in line with G1 foci observed in control cells.
source: Interestingly, in grand-daughter and great grand-daughter cells, the size of G1 foci increased (>2 µm2), in line with G1 foci observed in control cells (Figure 7A–C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells in mid-late S phase showed a large number of 53BP1 foci, which increased in size as cells progressed through the first G2 phase.
source: Finally, cells in mid-late S phase also showed a large number of 53BP1 foci, which increased in size as cells progressed through the first G2 phase.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The average number of 53BP1 foci in mid-S phase cells were higher and were removed later, just prior to mitotic entry compared to cells from early S phase.
source: Interestingly, the average number of 53BP1 foci in mid-S were higher and were removed later, just prior to mitotic entry compared to cells from early S phase (Figure 7A–C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The quality of mitosis was often reduced in cells from mid-S phase, with cells displaying chromatin bridges, micronuclei, and/or failed cytokinesis.
source: Furthermore, the quality of mitosis was often reduced in cells from mid-S phase, with cells displaying chromatin bridges, micronuclei, and/or failed cytokinesis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), correlating with the increase in death during or after mitosis we observed previously (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Figure 6C.

claim: Early S phase cells were able to either partially repair double-strand breaks during the first round of DNA replication and/or mark damage for efficient repair in the subsequent daughter and grand-daughter cells.
source: Based on these results, we concluded that early S phase cells were able to either partially repair double-strand breaks during the first round of DNA replication and/or mark damage for efficient repair in the subsequent daughter and grand-daughter cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 53BP1 foci analysis.

claim: Cells in G1 had much greater levels of damage and remained arrested in the first G2 phase after cisplatin exposure.
source: In contrast, cells in G1 had much greater levels of damage and remained arrested in the first G2 phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 53BP1 foci analysis.

claim: Cells in mid/late S phase completed the first division while acquiring damage but were unable to sufficiently repair the damage before mitosis.
source: Cells in mid/late S phase completed the first division while acquiring damage but were unable to sufficiently repair the damage before mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 53BP1 foci analysis and observation of mitotic defects.

claim: Daughter cells from mid/late S phase-treated cells with unrepaired damage had increased rates of mitotic induced breaks as they attempted the second round of DNA replication, leading to a strong S/G2 phase checkpoint arrest.
source: Consequently, daughter cells with unrepaired damage had increased rates of mitotic induced breaks as they attempted the second round of DNA replication, leading to a strong S/G2 phase checkpoint arrest, similar to cells initially exposed during G1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 53BP1 foci analysis and cell fate tracking data.

claim: Cells in early S phase were better able to take advantage of the high-fidelity HR pathway, whose activity peaks in mid-S phase.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesised that cells in early S phase were better able to take advantage of the high-fidelity HR pathway, whose activity peaks in mid-S phase (Karanam et al., 2012) compared to G1 or late S phase.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations, with citation to Karanam et al., 2012.

claim: Co-treatment with PARP inhibitor (olaparib) significantly reduced the total number of divisions in cisplatin-treated cells targeted in G1/S phase.
source: In cells treated with cisplatin, co-treatment with PARPi significantly reduced the total number of divisions (Figure 8B), indicating that cells were unable to continue proliferating.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Co-treatment with PARP inhibitor decreased the percentage of proliferative (two or more divisions) cells but only caused a small increase in death.
source: Interestingly, although co-treatment with PARPi decreased the percentage of proliferative (two or more divisions) cells, there was only a small increase in death observed (Figure 8D), indicating that PARPi alone is not sufficient to drive increased toxicity to cisplatin in A549 cells.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Inhibition of PARP increased the rate of 53BP1 foci formation compared to cisplatin alone in asynchronous cells.
source: Importantly, inhibition of PARP did increase the rate of 53BP1 foci formation compared to cisplatin alone in asynchronous cells (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: PARP inhibition correlated with a significant increase in both the amount of γ-H2AX staining and the size of cells.
source: Furthermore, this correlated with a significant increase in both the amount of γ-H2AX staining and the size of cells (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: RAD51 inhibition had no significant effect on cell growth compared to untreated controls.
source: RAD51 inhibition (RAD51i) had no significant effect on cell growth compared to untreated controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RAD51 inhibition resulted in a small but significant decrease in the number of divisions completed by early S phase cells treated with cisplatin.
source: Single-cell fate tracking of FUCCI expressing A549 cells revealed a small but significant decrease in the number of divisions completed by early S phase cells treated with RI-1 and cisplatin compared to cisplatin alone.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: RAD51 inhibition correlated with a reduction in percentage of cells completing two or more divisions (proliferative) and an increase in the percentage of cells undergoing a G2-exit phenotype.
source: This correlated with a reduction in percentage of cells completing two or more divisions (proliferative) and an increase in the percentage of cells undergoing a G2-exit phenotype (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Targeting DNA repair pathways during the first replication cycle results in more DSBs and pronounced S/G2 cell cycle checkpoint arrest leading to G2-exit.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that targeting DNA repair pathways during the first replication cycle results in more DSBs and pronounced S/G2 cell cycle checkpoint arrest leading to G2-exit, likely due to a reduced ability to repair DNA damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PARP and RAD51 inhibition experiments.

claim: Targeting DNA repair pathways reduces the ability of cells to undergo further rounds of replication and division.
source: This in turn reduces the ability of cells to undergo further rounds of replication and division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PARP and RAD51 inhibition experiments.

claim: A non-genetic, cell cycle-dependent mechanism of platinum resistance exists in lung adenocarcinoma.
source: In this work, we have identified a novel, non-genetic mechanism of resistance to platinum chemotherapy, which facilitates continued proliferation in a subset of LUAD cells after pulsed exposure to cisplatin.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: Cells in late G1/early S phase at the time of exposure had a greater proliferative capacity after pulsed cisplatin exposure.
source: Quantitative single-cell fate tracking revealed that cells in late G1/early S phase at the time of exposure had a greater proliferative capacity after pulsed cisplatin exposure.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by the FUCCI experiments and synchronization studies.

claim: Cell cycle stage at the time of exposure impacts how cells respond to cisplatin.
source: This suggests that cell cycle stage at the time of exposure impacts how cells respond to cisplatin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell cycle-dependent differences in response observed throughout the study.

claim: Cisplatin treatment of head and neck (UM-SCC-38) cancer cells resulted in similar heterogenous cell cycle and cell fate responses.
source: Interestingly, cisplatin treatment of head and neck (UM-SCC-38) cancer cells resulted in similar heterogenous cell cycle and cell fate responses (Luong et al., 2016), implying that the non-genetic cell cycle-dependent mechanisms of resistance we observed here may translate to multiple cancer types beyond LUAD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Luong et al., 2016.

claim: For cells in G1, the predominate response to cisplatin is to arrest in S/G2 during the first replication cycle.
source: For cells that are in G1, which under normal physiological conditions represents the vast majority of cells (>70%) both in vitro and in vivo, the predominate response is to arrest in S/G2 during the first replication cycle (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Intracellular pH is lowest during G1, and cisplatin DNA binding is markedly increased in acidic conditions.
source: Notably, intracellular pH is lowest during G1, and cisplatin DNA binding is markedly increased in acidic conditions (Stewart, 2007), hence cells in G1 phase at the time of exposure may have higher levels of cisplatin-DNA adducts.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stewart, 2007.

claim: Sustained S/G2 DNA damage has been shown to lead to ATR-mediated checkpoint signalling and sustained p21 expression, blocking CDK activity and preventing FOXM1-dependent G2 transcription required for mitotic entry.
source: Notably, sustained S/G2 DNA damage has been shown to lead to ATR-mediated checkpoint signalling and sustained p21 expression, blocking CDK activity and preventing FOXM1-dependent G2 transcription required for mitotic entry (Saldivar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saldivar et al., 2018.
